Georgia Affalrs.
A tremendous explosion occurred at the steam saw mill of Mr. A. P. Dixon, below Woodbury, in Meriwether county, last week. The boiler and heavy timbers and machinery were thrown hundreds of yards, and the tops of some of the tallest pines over fifty yards distant were broken off. No one was reported injured.

Mr. James Townsend, who, with his son, Mr. W. C. Townsend, has been planting rice at the LeConte place, in the lower portion of Liberty county, lost his barn and commissary by fire one night last week. The barn contained one thousand bushels of rice, which had just been threshed. The origin of the fire is unknown, but it is supposed to be the work of an incendiary.

Sneak thieves are walking off with cotton in Dublin.

The project of a cotton seed oil mill has been broached in Dublin.

Andrew Rivers, charged with the murder of Mrs. J. M. Clews and child, in Thomas county, a few months ago, has escaped from Valdosta jail, whither he was sent for safe keeping. It is thought he had help from outside.

The Griffin News learns that James F. White, who so cruelly shot Mr. James Rose, in Upson county, some weeks ago, has been captured, and will be speedily brought to justice. He was apprehended in Mobile county, Ala.

The Albany News and Advertiser reports that during the high wind of Saturday afternoon, a whirlwind struck a log cabin on Mr. Croff Mayo's Huger place, the sole occupant of which was Tom Lee, a negro blacksmith. A sill fell across his abdomen, and he died in two hours after being extricated from the debris. He was about fifty-five years of age, and had been in Mr. Mayo's employment some years. He had his leg amputated a few years ago.

The Augusta Evening News states that a little negro boy, Allen Moore, was committed by Recorder Webb Tuesday morning to await the action of the grand jury in a curious case of killing. Last May Allen was fighting with another small negro named Robert Griffin and struck the latter on the head with a brick. Griffin died three weeks since and the little fellow who caused his death is now committed for trial. He cannot be more than thirteen years of age and his parents say he is only ten.

Orange Law, a respectable colored man living near Riceboro, in Liberty county, had some money. Not having any confidence in banks since the days of the Freedman's Bank, he put his money in a trunk and hid the trunk under the shucks in his crib. Some one got the key of the crib to get some harness. Now Orange Law mourns the loss of his trunk and $315 in cash.

Sip Williams and Dublin Maberry, young gentlemen of color, are in Louisville jail regretting the fact that they tried their hand at burglary only to be caught.

A posse, led by officers Keyhoe and Ballard, made a raid in Gilmer county last week, and near M. V. Teems' destroyed a still and a quantity of beer, and in the Wheeler settlement, near the Gilmer and Pickens line, destroyed a still and about four thousand gallons of beer, besides capturing a barrel of whisky; also, on Talking Rock creek, in Pickens county, they made scraps of another still and liberated the fermenting contents of a number of spacious barrels to work its way down the famous stream.

The grading on the Marietta and North Georgia Railroad is moving up lively. The right of way is cut out to Cool Springs Church four miles from Jasper.

Information reached Washington on Sunday that two attempts had been made last week to turn the residence of Mr. Pleas. Cox, in Lincoln county. Five or six persons are said to be implicated. Some of them are negroes, and one or two are white men. Four negroes have been arrested, and were threatened with lynching. Messrs. F. H. Colley and M. P. Reese, of Washington, went down to Lincoln Monday to look into the matter. It is said that the plot was to burn Cox's house and kill him as he came out.

Thomasville Enterprise: "The dwelling house of M. E. W. Stephens on his plantation.
Tuomasville Enterprise: "The dwelling house of Mr. E. W. Stephens, on his plantation, near the station, in this county, was destroyed by fire last Saturday night. The fire, it is supposed, was the work of an incendiary, and one of Mr. Stephens' song narrowly escaped being burned in the house. The building was insured in the Southern Mutual for $700."

Hinesville Gaz ite: "We learn that the premises of Mr. W. A. Kennedy, a leading citizen in the upper part of the county, were destroyed by fire last Friday night. We are not in possession of any of the particulers, but are informed that the fire was the work of an incendiary who applied the torch to conceal theft. We are not able to state whether anything was saved."

Billjay Courier: "Bill Webb a few days since informed us that his brothers, Mart. and David, who live in Chattoooga county, this State, recently cut down a tree which was one hundred and sixty-five years old, each cut making thirteen hundred boards, numbering in all tourteen cuts. The boards are said to be worth $10. He says there is another tree standing near by which is larger than this one. He, in a sarcastic way, says Chattoooga is not a very good sect on for making boards."

Bulloch Banner: "Our farmers have suffered for the past two years from extended droughts, and now to add to the discomfiture of many there has been no timber here since the spring of 1881. Merchants and others are beginning to press their claims for debt, and there is a general cry of hard times."

Thomasville Times: "The election passed off quietly on Tuesday. The vote was not a very full one. The contest for Mayor was very close, Mr. Prevatt receiving 153 votes, and Judge Hopkins 152. The following gentlemen were elected Altermen: kedden P. Smith, Col. Wright, Jos Jerger, J. L Walcott, H. Wise and E. O. Thompson. It has been our custom to give the vote in full, but no one kept a copy, and consequently we cannot give it. The best of order and good feeling prevailed during the day. At night Mayor Prevatt and the board elect were serenaded by the band. Judge Hopkins has notified Mr. Prevatt that he will contest the election. The evidence will be taken before Judge Mitchell on Tuesday, when the managers will pass upon it."

Madison Madisonian: "Last Thursday evening the colored man carrier from this place to Monticello missed the mail bag. He immediately retraced his steps about two miles, and found the mail bag in the house of a colored woman named Amanda Jefferson. He brought it to this place, and the Postmaster discovered that the pouch had been cut open and riffed. The woman was immediately arrested and confined in jail. She says that her children found
it to this place, and the Postmaster discovered that the pouch had been cut open and riffed. The woman was immediately arrested and confined in jail. She says that her children found the pouch and carried it to her house, and that Charles Gary, colored, cut it open, she being absent from home at the time. A United States detective is in the city as we go to press ferreting out the guilty party."

Columbus Enquirer Sun; "A few days ago the Enquirer-Sun made a notice of the fact that the White colour Springs had been sold to Messrs. J. M. DeLacy and R. P. Talman, of Hatchechubbee, Ala. The next day the report was corrected, but we are now informed by both parties that the trade has been confirmed and the title has passed to the gentlemen above named. We repeat the opinion expressed a few days ago, that these gentlemen are successful business men and are full of vim and enterprise, with the capital to carry out what they undertake. We expect to see this favorite old summer resort what it used to be again by the coming summer, and, doubtless, before many years have roiled around their popularty will even be greater than ever before—and this is saying a great deal."

THREATENED LYNCHING.
Three Suspected House Burners in Peril in Lincoln County.
AUGUSTA, January 30 —There is considerable excitement in Lincoln county lately growing out of an attempt to burn the residence of P. A. Cox, within four miles of Lincolnton. Six negroes were arrested. Three were discharged, and Harry Kennedy, John Horry and Henry Wright were imprisoned. The firmness of the county officials saved the prisoners from lynching. Apprehension is still felt for their lives.

cal-jones-las-vegas-1882-02-04.A1:
A Shooting Affray. In which a negro by the name of Jake D. Smith was shot and killed by a Mexican. The shooting took place at the Plaza del Llano near the Hot Springs Saturday night about 12 o'clock. Desiderio Padilla done the shooting. The two ft seems had got into a quarrel. The negro received two pistol shots. One in the right breast a little below the nipple and the other above the left hip. The inquest was held on the body yesterday morning. The coroner's jury found that the deceased came to his death by pistol shots fired by Desiderio Padilla. Sheriff Romero went up yesterday morning to arrest the guilty party. Jake Smith, it is believed, is the man who murdered another negro in Cherry valley several years ago. At least there are parties in the neighborhood who are willing to swear that he is the murderer of Old Biles, as the negro killed at Cherry Valley was called. They Skipped.
For some time past there has been an evident accumulation of thugs and dead-beats in the city. The robbery of the discharged soldier the other day was the culmination of this lawlessness. And this also furnished a good excuse for the law-abiding citizens of the East Side to give the boys a few pointers. Consequently, about the hour of twelve Saturday night a goodly number of citizens gathered themselves together and took Cal. Jones, Tobe Johnson, Ed. Patters, a fellow by the name of Roxy and one that went by the euphoneous appellation of Buck, to a point a little north of the round house and proceeded to give the whelps a sligh' taste of how it goes to stand on nothing and kick at the United States. They were takes one by one and gently pulled up until their feet swung clear of the ground. This was repeated several times with each one, until it was thought they had received a sufficient foretaste of what remained in store for them if they persisted in remaining in town with no visible means of gaining a livelihood. When the noose was taken from their necks they lit out at a lively rate, avering that they had no especial business in this part of the country. This is a good les son for such fellows and the remedy can not be applied too often. Robbers and thugs of this stripe should not be tolerated in any community.

duffy-green-river-1882-01-21.A1:
A Utah Murder.
"California Bill," real name William Nugent, from Sacramento, Cal., was shot and instantly killed by William Duffy, at Blake City, Utah, Sunday, January 22.
duffy-green-river-1882-01-21.A2:
GLEANINGS FROM THE ROCKIES
According to the Virginia (New) Chronicle, the Government bonds, amounting to $7100, which the late John L. Moore of that city willed to his daughter, were found recently by J. W. Howard, his son-in-law, and Joseph Josephs. They were in a tin box, secreted in the attic of the old man's house, between the ceiling and the roof. The deceased refused during his sickness to tell where the bonds were. It was with great difficulty that he was induced to make a will at all.

Logan Leader: We learn of the very sad accident which occurred to Mr. Samuel Handy of Franklin on Sunday the 15th. A pair of his horses had broken loose and Mr. Handy mounted a young horse, and started after the runaway which he headed off about a mile from his house. He was seen coming back with them by his wife through the window. Soon after the three horses were seen by Mrs. Handy coming into the yard together. She wondered at this but supposed her husband had stopped on the way. As Mr. Handy did not return the wife instituted a search for him, when his dead body was found across the wagon road. The remaines were at once taken to the home of the deceased. An inquest was held before Justice Webster, and a verdict rendered to the effect that the deceased met with his death by falling from a horse and breaking his neck.

S. L. Tribune: Friday night when the treasurer of the Oates troup counted up the receipts of the house, he was somewhat taken aback at running across a bogns dollar. He hailed the door keeper, and showing him the money remarked that it was first time in all his nine years' experience with shows that he had ever been bitten with a counterfeit silver piece. Gold and greenbacks had at times gotten largely the best of him, but silver, never. Then he continued his count, and presently struck another, and another, and then he began to indulge in a regular typhoon of theatrical profanity. As the count continued the bogus dollars kept showing up a strong force until, lo and behold, there was just $75 in bogus coin that had been dumped into the opera bouffe exchequer. The probabilities are that everybody who found bogus dollars on their hands concluded that the shortest route to redemption was to patronize the theatre. Some probably thought that the counterfeit money was a stand-off for some of the padded calves in the chorus. In settling up accounts the local managers shouldered half the loss.

Ogden Pilot: Mrs Fred Nichols of Eagle Rock, met with a sad accident last week, while carrying a bucket of water, by falling across the bucket, fracturing the thigh bone and breaking some of her ribs. In the absence of a physician she had to be sent to Logan for treatment but her recovery is doubtful.

Invitations are out for another one of those enjoyable parties given by Mr. and Mrs. Clifford of Eagle Rock, for next Tuesday evening.

The Las Animas (Col.) Leader reports that an extensive prairie fire was raging last week between Butte and Bear creeks. It traveled about twenty miles a day and the flames were running high.

Register: The safe in the County Treasurer's office of Carbon county, Wyoming, was robbed last week, $2,100 in money, $300 in notes, $800 in checks and a Sweetwater county warrant for $136 was taken.

On Saturday last while the emigrant train of the Union Pacific Railroad was near Wasatch Station, a young girl, a passenger, named Nina Collins, stepped out onto one of the flat cars, when a sudden jerk of the train threw her off her feet, and falling between the cars, the coaches running over both legs above the knees, crushing them in a horrible manner. She was taken to Rawlins where her legs were amputated, but she only lived thirty-six hours. On the same day a brakesman named Jas. Brandolph while the train was near Filmore Station, stepped from one of the cars and fell under the wheels and was run over both legs being severed from the body at the groin. He died before assistance could reach him.

Evening News: By D. K. Reid of Castle Dale, Emery County, we are informed of the killing, on the 21st inst., of William Nugent, known as "California Bill," by William Duffy. The tragedy occurred at Blake City. The two had quarreled during the day, Duffy getting the worst of the fight. He subsequently procured a Winchester rifle with which he shot Nugent through the body, killing him. Nugent wounded Duffy in the calf of the leg, with a pistol shot. The affair raised quite an excitement, and threats of lynching Duffy were freely indulged in. This is the second homicide in Emery County within a very brief period, D. L. Blizzard being the previous victim.

Price River Notes.
PRICE RIVER CANYON,
February 10th, 1882.
Editors Herald:

Editors Herald:

I met a man in the canyon, today, on his way to Clear Creek, who claims to have been an eye witness to the shooting affray that took place at Green River on the 21st ult. From a short conversation with him I gleaned the following facts in relation to it: It appears that California Bill—whose right name is Wm. Neugent, from California—and Duffy were, in the phraseology of the place, "bunkeys," and shared the same bed; they were working for Neilson & Jensen, railroad contractors, east of Green River. On the day of the shooting they left camp together, quarreling all the way out over trivial matters; after they arrived in camp they indulged in several drinks together, but were by no means intoxicated, and quarreled again—over what I am unable to learn—and parted; but in a few minutes they returned, Bill with a pistol and Duffy with a rifle; as they met in front of Taylor's saloon, Bill fired on his former chum, the ball passing through the calf of his left leg; then Duffy raised his rifle and fired at Neugent, the ball entering his left breast and coming out under the shoulder blade; he fell backward through the doorway into the saloon and expired almost immediately. Duffy ran across the river, followed by a number of men, and after a short chase he was captured. It was only through the intercession of the cooler headed men that he escaped being lynched. He is now in the Provo Jail.

The people that constitute the better class of the population of this place are just awakening to the fact that a peaceable citizen's life will not be safe until some of the roughs that infest the country are made to perform the tight rope act and dance on nothing, for they continue to make things uncomfortably lively. On several occasions Mr. Forbs, who has charge of the D. and R. G. warehouse, has been run over the river at the muzzle of a gun by these playful scamps.

Two men were severely injured here on the 27th ult. They were working on the grade blasting rock; a blast was lighted, the fuse burned up, but the powder failed to ignite. They foolishly attempted to drill it out to save the powder, when it exploded, cutting them badly about the face and hands, one of them losing nearly the whole of his hand, and bruised their bodies considerably. They were sent to Salt Lake for repairs.

Clear Creek rejoiceth in a government postoffice, which is known as "Tucker" postoffice. FELIX.

Assinated by Hoodlums.
Assassinated by Hoodlums. CHICAGO, March 19.—On Friday night at Good Hope village, near Macombville, E. S. Edmondson, a prominent citizen was assassinated by three roughs whom he had turned over to the police a few days before for improper conduct. Ed. Gick was the man who fired the shots, and after his arrest there was difficulty in restraining people from lynching him.
ed-click-good-hope-1882-03-17.A2:
ASSASSINATED BY RUFFIANS.
CHICAGO, March 19.—Thomas Edmondson was killed on Friday by Edward Giek and two other ruffians whom he had arrested a few days before for improper conduct. Giek was arrested, but the other men escaped.
ed-click-good-hope-1882-03-17.A3:
A Steamer Blown Over on a Dam. The large stern-wheel steamer Montana, on her way from Pittsburg to St. Louis with a large miscellaneous cargo, was blown over on a dam at the head of the canal in Louisville: A portion of her hull is broken, but it is believed that she can be released. It will be necessary to dock her, however, before she can proceed on her voyage. The accident was caused by a blockade of coal barges at the entrance of the canal. Two European Theatres in Flames. In Marseilles, the Crystal Palace theatre
Two European Theatres in France.

In Marseilles, the Crystal Palace theatre has been destroyed by fire. The loss is 1,000,000 francs. The actors had great difficulty in effecting their escape from the burning building.

In St. Petersburg a fire broke out in the Winter Livadia theatre during the performance. So far as known no lives were lost.

Setting Forests on Fire.

It is believed that the fires started in the woods at Mastic, in the town of Brookhaven, N. Y., and which destroyed over fifty acres of valuable timber, were started by oyster thieves. Evidence has been secured against several persons, and a number of arrests are expected in a few days. The woods and houses are now guarded night and day.

Snow Blockade.

The snow blockade on the Central Pacific railroad continues. Advices from Emigrant Gap say that a snow plow, with eight engines, has cleared the road between Truckee and Blue Canon. Two sections of a western bound emigrant train and two plows are stuck between Atla and Blue Canon. One section of a western-bound passenger train is also lying there. It is now snowing.

Shad.

A shad, weighing $ \frac{5}{2} $ pounds, the largest of the season, caught off Weehawken on St. Patrick's day, was exhibited in Fulton market yesterday. The fisherman received $1 a pound for it. Fishermen say that shad will presently begin to run in numbers.

Disastrous Rains in South America.

Disastrous Rains in South America.

Rain has been falling in torrents during the last six weeks, doing great damage to railways in the provinces Rio de Janeiro, Sao Paulo and Minac Geraes. The towns of Sao Soao, Macahe, Paraty and Pirahi have been almost destroyed and many persons have been drowned.

Destructive Wild Fowl.

Many fields of grain in the Suscol hills, Cal., have been devastated by wild geese and ducks. The farmers have tried to keep the birds away by illuminating their fields at night with large lamps and having men ride around on horseback every few hours, but with little success.

Smallpox in Virginia.

Smallpox of a malignant type is prevailing in the negro settlement at Long Ridge, Norfolk county, Va., about 15 miles from Norfolk. Over 50 cases are reported and

many deaths. A colored man vaccinated himself and others with a seab from a smallpox patient and all thus inoculated died.

Killing Her Child While Drunk.
In New Brunswik, N. J., Nancy Bell, colored, while on a drunken carousal at her home, fell on her ten months' old child and killed it. She left the city before her arrest could be effected.

Result of an Old Grudge.

Result of an Old Grudge.

At Good Hope, Ill., Thomas Edmonson, an old and highly-respected citizen, was shot three times and almost instantly killed by a young man named Gick. The murder was prompted by an old grudge.

CRIMES.
Last Saturday night, at Hudson, Wis., Mrs. George Miles shot her husband while he was attempting to enter her residence on lower Second street, inflicting a painful but not dangerous wound. It seems the domestic relations of the unhappy pair have not been delightful since their marriage some thirteen years ago, because he was shiftless and cranky and she was hardly economical enough with her virtue for a well regulated helpmate. Mrs. Miles and Tobe Traverse werer arested on complaint of Miles, and taken before Justice Evans, the former charged with shooting, and the latter with being accessory. Both pleaded not guilty, and the state desiring more time, an adjournment was taken until the 23d inst., after which the prisoners gave bail for their appearance. Miles was so weak from loss of blood this noon that he was unable to sign his complaint.

James Ryan, a convict in the penitentiary a Stillwater, died Tuesday of consumption, and was buried in Fairview cemetery. James Ryan and James Toby were sentenced to the penitentiary for nine years from Dakota county, in 1877, for burglary, they having broken into and robbed a minister's house in Hastings. They were professional burglars and entire strangers in that part of the country. Toby died some two years ago, which was the last death in the institution until Tuesday, when his partner went to meet him.

Friday night, at Good Hope village, near Macombville, Ill., E. S. Edmondson, a prominent citizen, was assassinated by three roughs who he had turned over to the police a few days before for improper conduct. Ed. Gick was the man who fired the shots, and after he was arrested there was difficulty in restraining the people from lynching him.

Henry Renshaw armed himself with a brace of revolvers, and acting under the delusion that he was commissioned by divine authority in the name of Guiteau, made a murderous assault on Dr. Gray at Utica, N. Y. The doctor was not dangerously hurt. Like Guiteau, Renshaw was sane enough to seek the shelter of the Oneida jail immediately after firing the shot.

Ira Holmes, a well-known real estate man of Chicago, was robbed last Thursday of $12,000 of negotiable securities, being held up by footsteps on Wabash avenue. The affair was
Ira Holmes, a well-known real estate man of Chicago, was robbed last Thursday of $12,000 of negotiable securities, being held up by footpads on Wabash avenue. The affair was kept quiet, and the thieves, who proved to be three notorious crooks, were arrested, and the entire amount was recovered.

The three men arrested for complicity at Brussels in the Hatton Garden London, postoffice robbery, are believed to include the American Col. Gaston and his accomplice, who recently robbed a Paris jewelry house of 246,000 francs worth of goods.

S. Huston, a magistrate, and superintendent of construction on contract 42, Canada Pacific railway, at Eagle's lake, suicided at Rat Portage, Manitoba, by cutting his throat. The cause is believed to be domestic troubles.

The president ordered a further respite of thirty days in the case of Edward M. Kelly, sentenced to be hanged at Santa Fe, N. M., the 17th of February, and was then granted a respite until the 17th of March.

At Detroit, Mich., John M. Leonard, of Union City, was sentenced in the United States court to eight years in the house of correction for making and passing counterfeit money. Leonard is seventy-four years old.

Mrs. F. A. Reynolds, a widow, thirty-five years of age, employed in the Cleveland hospital for the insane, drowned herself.

An old man from Ontario was knocked down and robbed at night in the street at Winnipeg—the first crime of the kind in that place.
ed-click-good-hope-1882-03-17.A9:
NEWS MISCELLANY.
Events of the Day Briefly Chronicled.

The horse sheers of New York city will strike on Monday against the using of ready made shoes.

Free baths to the number of 2,617,112 were indulged in at New York during the season now about closed.

Robert E. Gick was yesterday convicted at Malcolm, Ill., of the murder of Thos. Edmundson at Good Hope in March last.

Thomas Riley, the well known swimmer, was yesterday discharged in the criminal court at Boston, where he had been on trial for the alleged larceny of a $1,000 bond.

A fire, yesterday, at Providence, R. I., in the drug warehouse of Oliver, Johnston & Co., resulted in a loss of $10,000. Stone & Murphy, tailors, also sustained a small loss.

The city insane asylum of New Orleans has been abolished, and 135 of its inmates, in charge of a large number of attendants, left last evening for the insane asylum at Jackson, La.

Henry J. Hall, late teller of the Rhode Island hospital trust company, yesterday, at Providence, pleaded non contendere to one of four indictments for embezzlement, and was sentenced to five years in the state prison.

James H. Elliott, the New York lawyer who was charged with burglariously entering the house of Emmeline Laurett and stealing a deed while she lay in bed attempting suicide by starvation, was yesterday discharged from arrest.

The discovery of a "meerschaum mine" is reported to have been made at Henry Station, N. C., at the foot of the Blue Ridge mountains.

Henry C. Carpenter, a prominent citizen of Russell county, Virginia, was yesterday assassinated near his residence by an unknown person.

Dr. Wirt Johnson, secretary of the Mississippi state board of health, has reliable information from Wesson, Miss., that there is no yellow fever there. Maggie Keppel, who is charged at Brooklyn, N. Y., with the abduction of little Lizzie Selden, was yesterday arraigned in court. She pleaded not guilty to the indictment found against her for abduction, with leave to withdraw her plea at any future time and offer one of insanity. Her trial was set down for the 17th of October.

STOVES, Etc. BBEECH LOADING GUNS. FINE BREECH LOADING GUNS!
The General Transatlantic Company of France started on the 4th the first steamer to ply regularly between Havre and Baltimore.

The Island of Anticosti, in the St. Lawrence River, containing more than 2,000,000 acres, is to be sold at auction, in settlement of a lawsuit.

Observations of the comet made at Harvard Observatory tend to establish the fact that it is one of a brief period, and that it is traveling at the rate of 400 miles per second. It has caused great consternation among the negroes of North Carolina, many of them firmly believing the end of the world is approaching.

George William Curtis is out in a letter asserting that Secretary Folger's ability and character are unquestioned, but the manner of his nomination was fraudulent; and believes the Republican voters in New York and Pennsylvania will repel the "unscrupulous cabals which bribe with public employment, and pay their way by filching from the public treasury."

The celebrated case of Mrs. Wackerle against the Mutual Life Insurance Company terminated on the 4th in favor of the widow, whose witnesses convinced the jury that her husband was really dead and her alleged spouse a fraud. The damages awarded are $6,506.99. It is believed the impersonator of Wackerle, deceased, will be apprehended by the United States authorities as a pension forger.

A temporary structure at St. Louis which had been erected for the purpose of viewing the Veiled Prophets' procession on the 4th, gave way under the weight of its occupants, and several persons were seriously if not fatally injured.

The recent census shows a population of 22,144,244 in the Austrian Empire, an increase of nearly two millions over the previous record.

The Irish police believe the murderers of Cavendish and Burke were ten in number, and are still in Ireland. The implements of the assassination were discovered a short time since.

Asiatic cholera is epidemic in many islands of the Malay Archipelago.

The Turkish Government has promised Greece that it will order an evacuation of all the ceded points without delay.

The Presbyterian churches of Philadelphia voted against the use of musical instruments during divine service, as destructive of the harmony of worship among the sect.

Captain John O'Connor, of Maryville, Mo., Postmaster, dealer in implements, and a prominent Greenbacker, is believed to have absconded, leaving deficiencies in his business and Postoffice accounts amounting to $20,000.

Adolph Marceaux became offended at Carencro, La., about some imagined wrong, got up a party of friends in military fashion and marched to a hall where a festival was being held. Arriving there, they opened fire on the assemblage, killing a girl named Domingue instantly and mortally wounding her brother. A sheriff and posse are hunting the assassins.

The Pennsylvania Steel Association held its annual session on the 4th at Philadelphia. The Secretary's report showed that the production had been increased 1,618,804 tons in ten years.

Secretary Teller on the 4th ordered the opening of the Turtle Mountain country for settlement.

Sixty miners had a narrow escape on the 4th from the Lehigh and Wilkesbarre Company's mine. The regular means of exit burned, and the men escaped through gangways leading to another mine. The agonizing cries of their relatives were pitiful, and some of the men fell senseless upon reaching the open air.

James Stainters, an employee of the Brush Electric Light Company, in New York, while adjusting a line on the 4th, received a shock which caused death almost instantly. The skin of his hands was seared off as if they had been burned.

There were fifty-five new cases of yellow fever at Pensacola on the 4th, and three deaths. Three new cases were bulletined at Brownsville.

The Dominion custom officers seized a large quantity of dry goods in the stores of prominent dealers at St. Stephen, N. B., on the 4th.

Alex H. Stephens was elected Governor of Georgia on the 4th. The returns indicate the success of the entire Democratic state ticket.

Will Rose, who left Danville, Ill., six weeks ago on a bicycle trip to San Francisco, has arrived at Cheyenne, Wy. T. He made 1,400 miles on his "wheel," and will proceed no further, fearing danger in the mountains.

Another death from smallpox is reported by the attending physicians near Prairie du Rocher, Randolph County. Of the ten unvaccinated cases in this group, six died, while of the vaccinated cases all recovered. A case of smallpox at Oglesby, LaSalle County, is reported by the president of the local board of health. The Mayor of Marshall, Clark County, reports a case a mile from town, contracted in Cincinnati. An eighteen-year-old boy called at police headquarters in New York on the 7th, and asked permission to carry a pistol, stating that he wished to shoot President Arthur. He was committed for examination as to his mental condition.

An Indignant Prosecuting Attorney.

Judge Shope's action in the Gick murder case, in changing the sentence from death by hanging to life confinement in the penitentiary, has aroused great popular indignation throughout McDonough County. William Prentiss, the State's Attorney, is out in a card in last week's Macomb Journal, in which he says:

His Honor tried the case well, as he is fully capable of doing. Up to the bringing in of the verdict, we have no fault to find, but from that moment he seems to have been completely unnerved. He evidently did not expect a verdict fixing the death penalty, and seems, judging from his subsequent conduct, to have determined that he would never pass sentence of death upon Gick if he could avoid it. From the dignified judge upon the bench, he became at once transformed into a back room supplicant in behalf of the criminal, apparently not so much to save the life of the culprit, as to relieve His Honor of the unpleasant duty of passing the death sentence. From that moment up to the time he finally accomplished his purpose, every power that his prolific brain could invent was brought to bear to compel the prosecution to submit to his terms. From Thursday until near noon Monday, at every opportunity, he sought to induce the prosecution to let Gick take a life sentence. He not only addressed himself to those directly connected with the prosecution, but to those who would be likely to have any influence upon them. He presented all the dangers and uncertainties of a new trial most forcibly. He stated, in substance, that rather than pass sentence of death on Gick, he would prefer to lose all his property. Still the prosecution adhered to the verdict, believing it to be just. Finally the widow of the murdered man was sent for, the prosecution refusing, under any circumstances, to agree that the verdict be set aside without her consent. The Judge then presented the case to her in his most forcible way (this was Monday forenoon and in the presence of Mr. L. B. Vose and myself). Mrs. Edmonson has never shown any spirit of revenge toward the murderer of her husband, although the loss has been greater to her than to anyone else. She simply wished the law to be executed, and as the matter of punishment was left to the jury, she desired their verdict to stand, and so told the Judge. Still His Honor persisted; he related how that he had written to his wife the evening before, that if he owned McDonough County he would give it all rather than pass sentence of death upon Gick. He then, in his most forcible and persuasive manner, called attention to the weak points in the record, remarking that if the Supreme Court wished to reverse the case and award a new trial, there were many grounds upon which to do it reasonably, and while he avoided saying so in so many words, he convinced Mrs. Edimonson, and all who heard him, including myself, that rather than pass sentence of death upon Gick he would himself grant a new trial. [SPECIAL TO THE SENTINEL.]
WASHINGTON, March 20.—It is understood that the friends of the Union and Central Pacific Railroad Companies are working vigorously against the passage of the Chinese bill in the House. They are interested in head money and also in Chinese labor.

Information About the Floods.

St. Louis, March 21.—The Clerk of the steamer City of Providence, just from Vicksburg, gives some information about the floods on the lower rivers not before published. He says the Parasol Steamboat Company, which runs steamers up the Yazoo river and its tributaries, is doing more to assist and rescue the people in that district than the Government and everybody else combined. It has sent into the submerged district of the Yazoo river, the Sunflower and the Tallahassee, the light-draft steamers Desmet and Headlight, equipped for special work. Each boat is supplied with a full complement of skiffs, axes and other necessary utensils. They steam into the flood as far as practicable, then anchor and send detachments in every direction to look for the sufferers. They have medicines, stimulants, etc., in each boat. The crews are started out in the morning, with instructions to prosecute their searches until nearly dark and then to return. The Sunflower, says the Clerk, returned the day he left Vicksburg. On board she had 350 sufferers, and her deck was crowded with cattle that had been picked up. The people on board were nearly all sick and a majority of them in destitute circumstances. Another of their boats, the Headlight, is expected back at any time. She will also be crowded with passengers and cattle. The worst point on the whole river is Milligan's Bend. There is an overflow and a counter overflow in that district. The waters from the Mississippi are going over the levee, and the floods and back-water from the Yazoo are coming in from behind. As a consequence where these two bodies meet a whirlpool is formed, which destroys everything in its course. The locality of the whirlpool is changing constantly, and every day it completes new destruction. A large yawl filled with negroes was caught in it the other day and upset, and all of the occupants drowned. The whirlpool struck a church a few days ago, in which several people with their stock had taken refuge. The church was in a few minutes torn to pieces, the stock was drowned and the people floated around in the water some hours, but were finally rescued. The vortex struck the residence and stable of an old paralytic farmer named Jameson, and totally annihilated them. The old gentleman was drowned.

Mass Meeting of the Trades Assembly.

CHICAGO, March 21.—A mass meeting of the Trades Assembly was held on Sunday, and adopted resolutions denouncing the Governor of Nebraska for calling out the militia against the Omaha strikers. A platform was adopted, declaring that every workingman should join the Union, which should fix wages and rates; denouncing "scabs" and Chinese, and those who patronize them; denouncing interference by the army, police, or militia, with their attempts to regulate wages; insisting on lower rents in Chicago; deploring the demoralized and venal character of the press, and declaring that the people should rise and regulate things. Making Subsidy Lands Taxable.
WASHINGTON, March 21.—A bill was introduced in the House yesterday by Representative Cassidy to compel a survey of the lands embraced within railroad subsidy limits. It sets forth that more than 25,000,000 acres remain unsurveyed of lands granted to the Central Pacific, Union Pacific and Kansas Pacific Railways, and that these companies, by their failure to cause a survey to be made, evade taxes in the States and Territories in which they lie, the revenues to which they are justly entitled. The bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to cause proper surveys to be made, and to issue land patents to the companies, and make the lands subject to taxation from the date of the execution of the patents. Referred to the Committee on Public Lands.

Moberay, an employee of the Denver & Rio Grande Railroad. Moberay owed the Mexicans $4, and of offered to pay them, but the latter demanded $8. The dispute resulted in the Mexicans beating Moberay, who shot them in self-defense. The high position of the Mexicans created a bitter feeling among this element, who were about to lynch Moberay. He was taken to the Chama jail for safety, from whence he escaped.

Quiet Restored at Omaha.

Omaha, March 21.—The relieving of the troops called here by the strike commenced last evening, when two companies returned home. Four companies of United States troops returned to Camp Sidney this morning. Grading is carried on with a full force, and there are no threats of interruption. Willows Springs distillery has filled the places of such employes as struck with new men. The smelting works have refused to take back men who quit voluntarily, and has reinforced the day and night shifts to nearly their full strength with new men.

A Grand Row at the Opera House.

PUEBLO (Col.), March 21.—Last night a free fight occurred among a crowd assembled at the Opera House to witness a wrestling match between a Leadville and a Denver man. The latter won. The Leadville men declared that the decision of the referee was unfair, and pulling their pistols, threatened his life. The Prospects of War in Europe.
LONDON, March 15.—The Times editorially says: War between Austria and Russia is always a possibility, but at present there is not, we trust, serious peril. The establishment of the Servian kingdon under Austrian auspices is an important guarantee of peace. Nor is a Slavonic storm likely yet to break upon Germany. We have reasons to believe that Bismarck has no fears in that direction, and he neither expects an attack nor intends to strike.

ST. PETERSBURG, March 21.—The General Staff have made a report, recognizing the impossibility of Russia waging an offensive war, and recommending that Warsaw and the western fortresses be strengthened against a possible invasion.

Occupation of the Balkans.

LONDON, March 16.—The Standard says: We can affirm that the Porte actually suggested to Bismarck the expediency of the occupation of the Balkans by Turkish troops, and that Bismarck replied that such measure was only permissible on the remote and violent hypothesis that there would be something like a concentration of Russian troops on the northern side of the range.

A Double Murder.
DALLES, March 18th.—A letter just received from Prineville, dated March 15th, contains the intelligence of the killing of two men on Willow Creek, in this county, by Lucian Langdon. The names of the men are A. H. Crooks and S. J. Jorry, a son-in-law of Crooks. The shooting was done just over a small knoll back of Langdon's house, a short distance from the road, and not discernible from it. Garret Maupis was passing the road at the time, heard the shots and some one say, "You have killed me." He went immediately where he heard the shots and found the two men dead and Langdon leaving on a horse, armed with a Winchester rifle. A poess will start in pursuit immediately. The trouble is supposed to have grown out of a lawsuit.

HORRIBLE WORK OF A MOB.
THE DALLES, March 19th.—Lucian Langdon and a man in his employ named Harrison were arrested at the residence of the former on Willow creek by a posse of citizens from Prineville, and turned over to Deputy Sheriff Lucky, who placed a guard of four men to protect them. Langdon requested the citizens making the arrest to guard him from mob violence, and the same request was made by his wife. This the party promised to do. Very soon after arriving at the Jackson House, about half-past 2 o'clock Friday morning the guard were overpowered by a masked mob of twelve or fifteen, who covered each member of the Deputy Sheriff's posse with a pistol and commenced shooting at Langdon, who was killed almost instantly. They then dragged Harrison to the Ochoco bridge, and hanged him to the trestle work. A Coroner's inquest was held over the dead bodies, and a verdict rendered according to the above facts. So far none of the perpetrators of this terrible outrage have been identified. Langdon leaves a wife and two young children. Nothing can be ascertained to implicate Harrison in the murder of Crooks and Jorry, and his only offense, it seems, was to have been employed by Langdon.
lucien-langdon-prineville-1882-03-17.A3:
The Wasco County Murder and Lethality
—Additional Particulars.
PORTLAND, MARYLAND, MAY 20, 1914.
Additional Particulars.

PORTLAND, March 20th. An Oregonian reporter to night interviewed a reliable gentleman just arrived from Prineville, Wasco county, and obtained the following additional particulars of the recent murder and lynching: A piece of land lying between the ranch of Crooks and Jorry and that of Langdon was in dispute. Langdon had fenced it in. On the 15th inst. Crooks and Jorry went on the disputed ground and began cutting a tree. When half done they were called to dinner. Upon their return they found Langdon cutting the same tree, with a shotgun near him. A quarrel ensued, when Langdon raised the gun, discharged both barrels, and killed the two men. The following Friday morning, when a Deputy Sheriff and a posse approached Langdon's house, they saw a man riding away. They headed him off, and ordered him to halt. He obeyed and surrendered himself, saying that he feared he would be lynched, and had mounted his horse with the intention of going to Prineville and giving himself up. That night he slept on a lounge in the parlor of the Jackson House with a guard of eight men. When the mob made their appearance the posse made no show of resistance. The Deputy Sheriff says a blanket was thrown over his head. The opinion prevails among many that the posse assisted in the lynching, though they had promised Langdon and his wife that he would be unharmed. The hanging of Harrison seems to have been a deliberate murder, as he was in no way connected with Langdon or the killing of Crooks and Jorry, but remarked when he heard of the affair, "Well, it is a good thing they were killed."

He was sleeping in the Jackson House when the mob approached, and having heard the shooting dressed and went down stairs to the street. Immediately a riata was thrown about his neck, the other end fastened to the pommel of a saddle, and the rider dashed away to Crooked river bridge, dragging Harrison, who was undoubtedly dead before the bridge was reached. The lynchers are supposed to be cowboys recently moved into the southern portion of Wasco county, and are prototypes of their brethren in Arizona and Texas.

GENERAL NEWS.
Robert Bailey, teacher in a schoo near Red Bud Illinois, was stabbed to death on Saturday, by a James E. McBride, a seventeen-year-old pupil, whom he was attempting to chastise for breach of discipline. McBride was arrested and held in $5000 bail to await the action of the Grand Jury.

The University Club House, 1316 Walnut street, Phila., Pa., was formally opened on Saturday. Bishop Stevens, the President, and others making addresses. The club is purely social, and it is requisite that a member shall be a college graduate.

Edward E. Blanchard, aged 29 years, Assistant Teller of the Farmers and Mechanics' National Bank of Buffalo, disappeared about a week ago, with money belonging to the bank. Wine, women and gambling caused his ruin.

A sub-committee of the House Committee on Territories unanimously agreed on Saturday to report favorably to the full committee the bill for the establishment of the Territory of North Dakota, and providing a temporary government therefor.

George Payne, well known to visitors of museums throughout the United States as "the man without arms," died last Thursday at his home in Williamsburg, New York, aged 27 years. From his birth he was compelled to make his legs and toes go service for arms and hands, and he fed himself like other people. He also shaved himself and was a good penman. He leaves a wife and child.

About three days of this kind of weather will make ice of sufficient thickness to cut for summer use.

The police raided a house of ill-fame on Saturday night and captured the inmates. The proprietress was required to pay $80 and costs by the Mayor.

A delegation of prominent citizens of Dakota, about 75 in number, passed through Chicago yesterday, on their way to Washington, to urge the admission of the southern part of that Territory as a State.

The present population of Chicago is estimated in that city at about 630,000, or 125,000 more than in 1880, when the last census was taken.

Rev. Father Grace, of Pittsburg, stated last evening that, at the recent conference of the Catholic clergy of that
The Irish American National Executive Committee in Chicago has issued an address naming the 22d of February as a day to be appropriately celebrated by the Irish in the United States, it being not only Washington's birthday but the aniversary of the demand made by Grattan for the independence of the Irish Parliament. The committee suggests that "in lieu of unsightly processions, banquets, etc., on next St. Patrick's Day the Irish in America assess themselves for what would be the cost of regalia, flags, music and caterers, and transmit the amount at once to redeem the pledge of $250,000 made at the Chicago Convention.

A boy named W. H McLoughlin, at Boston, was shot dead by a police officer, on the 22d inst. The officer was endeavoring to arrest the boy for beating his sister, when he attacked the officer and met his death.

Michael Rourke murdered an old man named Mayer and his daughter at Cumminsville, Canada, on the 21st inst. The murderer boarded with his victims.

Miss Betay Bland, residing near Lancaster, Ky., was murdered by a dissolute nephew named Wm. Austin. Robbery was the motive.

A mob took Henry Wagoner, who murdered Dr. Beynes, paymaster of the Ironton, O., iron works, from jail at that point on the 20th inst., and hung him.

Scattle, Washington Territory, had a sensation, on the 19th inst., when a mob took Benj. Payne, accused with murder, from the officers and hung him.

Mrs. Wm. Smith, a crazy woman, shot her husband, at Mt. Joy, N. J., on the night of the 18th inst., killing oim instantly.

James A. Wilmot, a farmer, living near Louisville, Ky., in a moment of insanity, on the night of the 18th inst., killed his aged mother, his wife and two daughters and then hanged himself. His oldest son had a terrible struggle with his father and barely escaped with his life.

In a shooting affray at Jackson, Texas, on the 17th inst., Lester Upham was instantly killed and P. Walworth, seriously wounded.

During a saloon row at Rayville, La., on the 18th inst., Wm. T. Little, a white man, blew off the head of a colored man named Milus Matthew, with a shot-gun.

A pawnbroker named Frank Semons was found murdered in his store at Kansas City, on the morning of the 16th inst.

Daniel Smith, of Richmond, Ind., has confessed that he murdered his father and threw the body into the well.

William Brocksmit, of Cedar Rapids, Ia., aged 19, was murdered on his sheep ranche, in New Mexico, on the 14th inst., by unknown parties.

The discharged jurymen in the Guiteau case must feel a good deal like soul's just out of Purgatoy. Their lives have not of late been cast in pleasant places.

George Gist and Samuel Cooper, both arrested by Officers Martin and Mahanny for drunkenness, were each fined one dollar and costs by Magistrate Comings yesterday.

Mr. Charles C. Mason, for a long time one of the clerks in the Illinois Central railroad office, was promoted to the chief clerkship in that office a few days ago.

The raffle of the fancy buffalo horn chair of Mr. J. W. Everly took place at Mr. O'Hara's drug store, on Tuesday of this week. Number twenty-two proved to be the lucky number, and it was held by Mr. Wm. Wolfe, of the New York store.

The ferryboat, Three States, will make a grand excursion trip to Wickliffe Sunday afternoon, leaving the wharf at two o'clock and remaining at Wickliffe long enough for excursionists to view the town. Round trip 25 cents.

Number one of volume one of the Wickliffe Tribune has reached this office. It is a six column folio, published weekly by Mr. H. F. Thurman. It has a much better appearance than country papers usually have. It is welcomed to THE BULLETIN's exchange table and deserves to prosper.

The sewer crossing Fourteenth street, on the east side of Poplar, has caved in, causing a hole near the centre of the street of about three feet deep and four feet in diameter. It has been baricaded, however, to avoid accidents and will doubtless be filled up and the sewer repaired as soon as the weather will permit.

—A lady named Mrs. Dennis O'Brien, living in the Clark block, on Ohio levee, died yesterday about noon, and will be taken to Grand Chain for burial to-day. She was the mother of a numerous family of children, one of whom is employed as "devil" in THE BULLETIN composing-room.

—A white man named Jacob McEwen and a negro were out in a canoe on the back water, just below Belmont, on Wednesday, and, in an unguarded moment they lost their balance, turned the canoe over, and the white man was drowned. The negro saved himself by clinging to the overturned canoe until help came to him.

—One thousand dollars worth of mules, belonging to Mr. Frank Crossno, a Mississippi county, Mo., farmer, died from the effects of being driven through cold back water a day or two ago. They were on a ridge surrounded by water, and Mr. Crossno drove them through the water to his stables with the result as stated.

—The Illinois Central railroad has a large force of men constantly at work in the railroad yards, repairing the company's tracks. Continued wet weather has had an injurious effect upon the ties and much traffic has done upon the same for the rails, hence the urgent necessity for extensive repairs.

—An item is going the rounds to the effect that a fortune-teller drove a woman crazy in Buffalo, N. Y., the other day. Not for the sake of the fortune-teller profession, but for the sake of truth, we feel like starting the suspicion that the woman was crazy before she went to the clairvoyant's house. She must have been.

The steamer John B. Maude attempted to cross over the made land on the Mississippi side of Cairo yesterday morning into the channel, but when she reached a point about opposite the slaughter houses, she ran aground right in a corn field. All the power of her mighty engines was not equal to the task of pulling her off again, and the Port Eads went to her assistance and drew her off.

A school master near Red Bud, a station on the Cairo & St. Louis narrow gauge railroad, last week attempted to administer bodily punishment to a pupil, eighteen years of age. The boy resisted, and in the struggle which ensued, stabbed the teacher with a sharply pointed lead pencil. The teacher died within a few minutes, death being caused by the excessive bleeding of the wound.

Officer Haz. Martin arrested Andy Forbes yesterday for keeping a second-hand goods establishment without having first procured a license from the city to do so. Forbes was fined ten dollars and costs by Magistrate Comings. Wm. Morgan, arrested by officer Mahanny for disorderly conduct, was fined five dollars and costs by the same court.

The young man McBride, who stabbed his school teacher, Bailey, near Red Bud a few days ago was arrested and taken to Waterloo on Sunday, the 22nd inst. Having waived examination there, he was committed to jail to await the March term of the circuit court. On Mondaya large and excited crowd assembled near the jail and threatened lynching, but they did not attempt to carry out their threats.

Two saloons have opened up business just outside the town limits of the town of Sparta. The town of Sparta is a red-hot temperance town, where the sale of liquor is prohibited by act of the town board, and the temperance people of the place are exceeding wroth at the audacity of the "two new saloon keepers," as the Sparta Plain-dealer calls them. One of these saloon-keepers, says the Plaindealer, "not only sells but manufactures the vilest kinds of liquors.

A number of cities in this state have increased the amount of yearly saloon licenses in order to raise more money for the necessities of the municipal government. The idea seems to be constantly spreading, too. Chicago started the ball and a number of smaller towns in southern and central Illinois took it up. The latest agitation of the matter is in Springfield, where the Journal urges the propriety of raising the saloon license in order to meet the expense of improving streets etc.

Mr. C. H. Warner, of the Quincy, (Ill.), telephone exchange assumed charge of the Cairo telephone exchange yesterday morning, relieving Mr. R. P. Hotchkiss, who has had the management of the latter for some time past and given general satisfaction. Mr. Warner is an old telegraph man and an experienced electrician, who has been connected with the management of telephones ever since their invention. Mr. Hotchkiss will be made superintendent of telephones of the southern portion of Illinois, with headquarters at Springfield.

Two houses floated by the city in the Ohio river yesterday morning about nine o'clock. But little more than the roofs were visible. They were small houses, not worth above fifty dollars when new; but tears of commiseration filled the eyes of tender hearted spectators on the levee, at the sad thought that the best business and residence portion of Paducah was being thus little by little carried down the remorseless stream, leaving the poor inhabitants no alternative but to get astride of a plank and come to Cairo for refuge.

Mayor Harrison, of Chicago, issued an order the other day that all gambling houses should close Saturday night at 7 o'clock. The object of this was not to trouble the gamblers, but to protect the wages of the working classes from the keno fiend and faro sharp. Promptly at the hour named last Saturday night the police served these notices and the gamblers without exception closed up. The thing worked like a charm, because the gamblers didn't resist. The gamblers say they don't object. They don't want the money of working-men. They want customers with more fat in them. Hereafter the rule will be enforced every Saturday. Nothing is said about the rest of the week, but the inference is that the houses are not to be molested as long as they allow the good wives to have the first shy at the weekly salaries of clerks and laborers.

High Water in Tennessee. NASHVILLE, January 24.—The river continues to fall slowly. The damage done by this rise is estimated at $400,-000. John Drake (colored) was drowned last night; no other lives have been lost in the city. At noon there was fifty-three feet four inches, showing a decrease of one foot eight inches. This is given up to be the highest rise in the Cumberland in the history of Nashville. Telegraphic reports state that the Tennessee river is rising. No trains over the Northwest division as yet, and it will be several days before they resume. The poor fund has reached about $12,000. Clinching Their Election. Since last week we have obtained fuller information concerning the killing of Sol. Waters by William Parish, which occurred on Monday, February 20th. It seems that Waters, in order to decide the dispute concerning the deer skin, had taken out his razor and was cutting the skin in half, when Parish seized Waters' shot-gun and fired on him while he was in the act of stooping. A load of fifteen buckshot penetrated Waters' body, entering at the back and going through the lungs.

Parish spoke about it in a brutal manner, saying he did not care any more about killing a negro or a white man than about eating his dinner; and moreover, his punishment would only consist in working on the levee.

Between 2 and 3 a. m. on Friday last, while Parish was chained to a tree in the yard of Captain S. D. S. Newell's former residence in Newellton, a body of masked men, about fifteen or twenty in number, seized Parish, and stuffing his mouth full of cotton to smother his cries, hung him to a tree in front of Dr. Percy's office in Newellton. We are informed, however, that Parish was strangled to death before he was swung to the tree. The coroner's inquest held on Parish's body resulted in the finding of a verdict by the jury to the effect that the deceased had met his death by strangulation at the hands of men unknown to the jury.
